overview: The atlas paints “Tibeto-Burmanese” across a huge slice of High Asia from 2000 to 1500 BCE. That catchy label is the map editor’s umbrella, not the name of a known people, country, language, or border. Its polygon includes Nagqu, Qamdo, Nyingchi, Yushu and even Hotan, yet leaves out Lhasa, Kathmandu and much of the eastern Himalaya. Archaeology is patchier and more interesting. Near and beyond that outline, communities fished cold lakes, hunted, tended millet fields, adopted barley and wheat, managed sheep and goats, shaped stone and bone, made pots, and exchanged materials along valleys and grasslands, but never all in the same way. A fun scientific clue comes from ancient tooth crust: proteins can reveal milk, although the first direct goat-milk result here dates just after the card ends. New radiocarbon work can also ruin a neat tale in the best possible way: Qugong, once assigned to this span, now dates around 1400 to 1300 BCE. Language-family trees remain debated, and no object tells us its maker’s speech. At 1500 BCE the atlas replaces this shape with several other labels. People and lifeways continued; only the oversized category vanished.

periods.title: A painted border, not a Bronze Age nation
periods.summary: The atlas begins one enormous polygon at 2000 BCE. Directly dated barley appears near the northeastern plateau margin, while Zongri interaction and Karuo’s final occupation belong to particular landscapes. None identifies a Tibeto-Burman state, ethnicity or language territory.

periods.title: Regional sequences refuse one clock
periods.summary: Archaeological chronologies differ across Qamdo, Qinghai, the high interior and Himalayan margins. The fifty-year window keeps the atlas lifetime continuous, but it is an editorial ruler mark rather than a named phase witnessed simultaneously across the polygon.

periods.title: People, herds and uncertain milk at Gepaseru
periods.summary: A Gepaseru individual dates about 1883 to 1691 BCE, with sheep and goat skulls nearby. Poor calculus preservation prevents direct milk-protein proof for that person. The cemetery also lies south of the atlas polygon, making it illuminating regional context rather than a target-wide fact.

periods.title: Caprines spread through neighboring corridors
periods.summary: Direct dates in the Tao River Valley place domestic sheep around 1900 to 1750 BCE. That valley is outside most of the drawn shape, yet shows how animals and practices moved through connected northwest regions without carrying a guaranteed language or ethnic identity.

periods.title: Cold highlands reward mixed strategies
periods.summary: Fields, herds, hunting, gathering and exchange offered different buffers against frost and drought. Evidence varies sharply by elevation and basin; environmental and archaeological models support mosaics of practice rather than one synchronized conversion from foraging to farming.

periods.title: An eastern evidence gap matters
periods.summary: Research identifies a settlement and radiocarbon gap around 2000 to 1700 BCE on parts of the eastern plateau. An empty excavation record does not mean an empty land. Mobile use, erosion, limited survey and poor preservation all remain possible explanations.

periods.title: Barley, wheat and livestock gain importance
periods.summary: After roughly 3600 years before present, cold-tolerant cereals and animals supported more sustained use of higher elevations. The pattern developed unevenly and often near or outside the atlas edge; it cannot be converted into a migration of one named language community.

periods.title: Thin dates replace confident guesses
periods.summary: A dating audit of twelve Yushu sites found only one securely Bronze Age human sample; many presumed prehistoric remains proved historical. That is not failure. It demonstrates why direct dating must outrank pottery labels and why this map needs visible uncertainty.

periods.title: Connected regions, still distinct communities
periods.summary: Crop routes, animals, pottery and eventually metals connected northern, eastern, central and Himalayan zones. Different evidence traveled by different paths. Similar objects may reflect exchange or imitation, while ancient genomes reveal interaction without supplying language names.

periods.title: The category ends; histories continue
periods.summary: At 1500 BCE the exact atlas id disappears and other broad labels divide its former sampled points. Qugong’s newly modeled deposits begin later, around 1400 to 1300 BCE, and direct goat-milk protein also falls mostly after the boundary. The seam is editorial, not a collapse.

sections.title: Unpaint the map before meeting the people

items.text: The live index names this exact record “Tibeto-Burmanese,” calls it a culture, and gives approximate dates of 2000 to 1500 BCE. Those are database fields, not ancient testimony. No inscription, ruler list, capital, census or self-name establishes a society by that name.

The sole polygon is one nine-point shape spanning about 73.5° to 99.7°E and 25.2° to 37.8°N. It owns sampled Nagqu, Qamdo, Nyingchi, Yushu and Hotan, yet excludes Lhasa, Shigatse, Kathmandu and much territory where related languages are spoken today.

At 1500 BCE the exact id vanishes. Sampled places are redistributed among atlas labels such as “Tibetans,” “Burmese,” “Dravidians” and others, often with radically changed coverage. That redraw is not evidence of conquest, migration, language replacement or four clean successor peoples.

“Tibeto-Burman” is a linguistic classification with hundreds of diverse languages and disputed internal branching. Even scholars who accept a Sinitic versus Tibeto-Burman split do not thereby create one prehistoric people. Languages can spread through learning, marriage, trade and political change.

Archaeologists instead work from named sites, layers, objects, bones, plants and dates. The current synthesis treats transformations after 2000 BCE as regional processes. This card follows that method: every example keeps its locality and never turns a language-tree branch into a territorial border.

Radiocarbon dates estimate when once-living material stopped exchanging carbon with the atmosphere. Researchers calibrate results and compare them with stratigraphy. A date belongs to the sampled seed, bone or charcoal, not automatically to every artifact, wall or person found nearby.

Qugong once anchored a 2000/1750 to 1500 BCE story. Seven new dates plus stratigraphic Bayesian modeling now place its relevant deposits around 1400 to 1300 BCE, after this card. Science did not “lose” a site; it gained a sharper clock and exposed how inherited chronologies can mislead.

Optically stimulated luminescence can date when mineral grains were last exposed to light before burial. It is especially helpful when stone artifacts lack charcoal, but sediment movement and landform history matter. A glowing laboratory signal still needs a secure archaeological context.

Ancient DNA can reveal biological relationships and population interaction. Plateau genomes show strong regional structure as well as shared ancestry. Genes do not encode pottery style, political loyalty or spoken language, so “genetically related” must never be rewritten as “the same Tibeto-Burman people.”

At Mabu Co, excavation, isotopes, animal and plant remains, tools and DNA combine to reconstruct a lake-centered life around 2450 to 2050 BCE. The site is just before this interval and outside the strict polygon; it supplies a nearby predecessor case, not a universal opening scene.

sections.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments

items.text: The polygon crosses high steppe, cold desert, river valleys, basins and eastern mountain margins. Water, snow, growing season and fuel differ enormously across those settings. A later ecological survey helps describe the physical mosaic, but it is comparison rather than a Bronze Age census.

Nwya Devu lies inside the mapped shape and preserves high-altitude stone-working tens of thousands of years earlier. Its importance is deep human experience on the plateau, not direct ancestry for a 2000 BCE community. A very old campsite cannot name a much later language.

Chusang hand- and footprints show another much earlier episode of central-plateau use. Competing date interpretations remind us that spectacular traces still require careful geology and chronometry. The prints are human and moving; they are not signatures saying what their makers called themselves.

Present-day high-altitude physiology includes a Denisovan-related EPAS1 variant, and ancient research places selected variants deep in plateau history. That explains biological adaptation at population scale. Without a sampled genome, it cannot identify the breath, ancestry or language of an individual potter.

Pollen, charcoal and sediments record vegetation, fire and landscape change over long spans. They show that agropastoral landscapes emerged through repeated human-environment interaction over centuries. They do not reveal a single arrival day when everyone suddenly became a farmer or herder.

Karuo near Qamdo preserves houses, roads, ash pits, pottery, stone and bone tools, millet and animal remains, but its accepted range ends around 2100 BCE. It is a close predecessor inside the polygon, useful for inherited skills and questions, not proof that identical households survived unchanged.

Near the northeastern plateau margin, directly dated barley appears around 2000 BCE. Crop genetics suggests several possible eastward routes. One grain can establish presence at a site; it cannot by itself reveal whether seed arrived through migrating farmers, neighbors, exchange or experimentation.

Millet favored warmer lower valleys, while barley and wheat later made colder elevations more farmable. Archaeobotanical syntheses nevertheless show mixed systems and large gaps across seasons. Families could combine crops rather than swap one complete “civilization package” for another overnight.

Domestic sheep are directly dated in the Tao River Valley around 1900 to 1750 BCE, with goats later. Animals provided meat, hides, fiber and perhaps milk, but this evidence lies east of much of the map. A traveling sheep carries no tiny passport naming its owner’s language.

Gepaseru offers the interval’s funniest serious clue: hardened tooth plaque survived when food did not. The earliest individual, dated about 1883 to 1691 BCE, lacked enough preserved calculus for milk-protein testing; nearby sheep and goat skulls suggest possible milking, while direct goat protein is later.

sections.title: Homes, water, fire and the toilet question

items.text: No excavated floor plan represents every community inside this polygon. Karuo’s earlier substantial buildings contrast with mobile or poorly preserved traces elsewhere, and later Qaidam sites include small structures. Houses may have used stone, earth, timber or perishable materials according to local supply.

Cold households needed fuel for cooking and warmth. Charcoal and combustion studies can identify burned woody plants, shrubs or dung-like materials, but choices varied with ecology. A hearth assemblage records what reached one fire; it is not a plateau-wide fuel rule.

Water came from rivers, springs, lakes, snowmelt and stored supplies, depending on season and place. The archaeological sources do not document one in-period canal or household water code for this umbrella. Fetching, protecting and sharing water were necessary, but exact duties remain unknown.

Ash pits and refuse deposits help archaeologists reconstruct food, fuel and broken tools. Their contents can mix through cleaning, animals or later disturbance. A rubbish hollow is valuable evidence, yet it is not automatically a kitchen, ritual deposit or carefully engineered sanitation system.

No securely dated toilet, latrine or sewer belongs to this exact atlas layer. Human waste may have been deposited away from living and water areas, but no universal practice is preserved. The honest answer is less glamorous than invented plumbing: archaeologists have not found enough.

No text lists households, marriages or inheritance rules. Graves and genomes can sometimes identify biological relatives, while settlements show shared work, but neither captures adoption, friendship or every kind of family. Household organization almost certainly varied among valleys, camps and generations.

Women and men both contributed to survival, yet tools rarely announce a worker’s gender. Later textile evidence shows skilled spinning and weaving, but spindle whorls alone cannot prove who spun. Tasks may have followed age, ability, season, household custom or status.

Children learned safe routes, weather signs, animals, plants, tool handling, cooking and social obligations by watching and practicing. No school building, alphabet lesson or timetable survives for this layer. Learning is a strong household inference, while formal education would be an unsupported invention.

Mabu Co’s bone needles, fish-gorge hooks, pottery and stone tools reveal sequences that require teaching and repeated practice. Because the site predates the card, it demonstrates available regional knowledge without proving that every 1800 BCE child learned fishing or sewing.

Ancient genetic samples show regional continuity and interaction, not sealed bloodlines. Marriage could have linked communities, but genomes do not disclose affection, consent, residence rules or spoken language. A biological connection is one strand of social history, never the whole family story.

sections.title: Tools, pots, cloth and practiced hands

items.text: Stone remained useful beside new metals. Knappers selected raw material, struck flakes and resharpened edges; polished tools demanded grinding. Luminescence, use-wear and residue studies can date or test activities, but a tool type alone cannot supply its maker’s ethnicity or mother tongue.

Pottery stored, cooked and carried food and water. Similar forms can spread by exchange, imitation or shared practical needs, while local clays and tempers expose different production choices. Archaeologists compare whole assemblages and layers rather than treating one decorated sherd as an ethnic badge.

Spindle whorls and fabric traces from the southeastern plateau show that spinning and weaving were skilled technologies, although much evidence belongs later. Cloth decays, so the surviving sample is biased. Wool, hair, hides and plant fibers remain possibilities only where direct traces support them.

Copper and bronze appear unevenly across northwest and eastern plateau regions. Qijia-associated metallurgy changed from early copper-working to more tin bronze around 1700 to 1500 BCE, but different local sequences overlap. Metal knowledge traveled; it did not draw this atlas polygon.

At Changguogou, reported barley, wheat and foxtail millet show demanding knowledge of planting, harvesting, storage and processing. The site’s position outside the strict polygon and uncertain older chronology make it regional comparison. Its crops cannot feed every household painted on the map.

sections.title: Movement, exchange and conflict without an empire

items.text: Valleys and grassland passes linked ecological zones. Crop varieties, livestock, pottery ideas and stone or metal materials could move in stages between neighbors. Geospatial models propose interaction corridors; they are testable reconstructions, not recorded roads, borders or royal transport plans.

Zongri combines foraging evidence, cultivated plants, animal remains and ceramics that reflect exchange near the northeastern margin. That mixture shows people could borrow foods and objects without becoming one identical culture. Contact leaves overlapping traces rather than tidy color blocks.

Barley and wheat followed different routes and flowering adaptations across Eurasia. Their arrival on plateau margins belongs to crop history, not a single human migration. Seed can travel through many hands, and farmers can adopt a plant while retaining other languages and traditions.

Metal weapons eventually appear in neighboring regions, but no army is shown controlling this polygon between 2000 and 1500 BCE. Hunting gear, personal defense, raiding and organized warfare can overlap materially. Without trauma, fortifications or settlement patterns, scale and coercion remain uncertain.

The map reaches Hotan while excluding many Himalayan and southeastern places associated with related languages today. That odd seam itself disproves literal reading. It is a modern editorial shortcut across exchange zones, not a surveyed frontier that ancient families guarded or crossed at checkpoints.

Thin air, cold, smoke, falls, infection, hunger and childbirth could harm people. Ancient bones and teeth can show stress, injury or disease, while healing suggests survival with time and perhaps care. They rarely identify the herb, food, helper or ritual that aided recovery.

Dental calculus preserves proteins because plaque mineralizes. Laboratory controls distinguish ancient peptides and assess preservation in one sample. Direct evidence is powerful, but absence is tricky: the earliest Gepaseru calculus was too poorly preserved, so “no detected milk” cannot become “no dairy.”

Baishiya Cave animal bones and proteins demonstrate how zooarchaeology and proteomics can reconstruct subsistence in deep time. Those Denisovan-era findings are vastly earlier than this card. They teach a method, not a belief system or direct family line for Bronze Age communities.

Burials may preserve body position, offerings, ornaments and relationships among graves. Later Sding Chung cave evidence proves mortuary practices varied across the plateau. It cannot be pasted backward as this interval’s religion, and grave goods never translate themselves into a complete theology.

Sheep or goat remains beside a burial may reflect food, offering, herd wealth or several meanings. At Gepaseru, skulls help establish animal presence but do not name a god or ritual sentence. Belief must stay an open question when texts and secure repeated patterns are absent.

Language phylogenies reconstruct relationships from systematic sound and vocabulary correspondences. One model estimates a northern farming-linked origin around 7200 years before present; another favors a later mean near 5900 years. Neither can place a named language inside this exact polygon in 1800 BCE.

A third clock analysis produces a very broad root-age interval and different subgroup support. That disagreement is useful: models depend on language samples, cognate judgments, calibrations and tree assumptions. “Proto-Tibeto-Burman” is a reconstruction, not a recorded speaker community or archaeological culture.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is responsibly attributable to this record between 2000 and 1500 BCE. Old Tibetan documents begin in the imperial era, and the earliest Burmese texts are later still. Borrowing either script, a modern phrase or an oracle-bone character would fabricate a voice.

The real achievements were plural: surviving altitude, combining foods, tending animals, reading seasons, crafting stone, bone, pottery and cloth, and maintaining exchange across difficult terrain. These accomplishments belonged to many local communities, including people whose languages and names remain unknown.

At 1500 BCE the atlas removes one umbrella and paints several new ones. No archaeological evidence shows that one Tibeto-Burmanese civilization fell. Households, routes, crops, herds and local traditions continued changing, while much later Tibetan, Burmese and other language histories developed on their own timelines.

ending.text: The exact atlas id disappears at 1500 BCE, when its sampled territory is redistributed among several other broad labels. That is a cartographic seam, not the fall of a state or disappearance of a people. Archaeological communities, routes, farming, herding and foraging continued locally. Newly dated Qugong deposits and direct goat-milk proteins mostly begin after this endpoint, illustrating why later evidence must not be pulled backward. No automatic predecessor or successor is defensible for an anachronistic language-family umbrella.
